name: Dea Nutrix
sources: Straffon, Cheryl. The Earth Goddess: Celtic and Pagan Legacy of the Landscape. London: Blandford, 1997.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Dea Nutrix is a British and continental Celtic goddess of nourishment. The name is Latin for "nourishing goddess." Excavations in the temples of Roman Britain have yielded dozens of small pipe-clay statuettes. These figures are usually three similar women holding fruit, eggs, grain, children, and other symbols of abundance and fertility. They may be related to the Deae Matres, the triple Divine Mothers. When the same goddess appears alone, she often nurses an infant. Both forms stress her link to food. The original Celtic name for these divinities is lost, so scholars use the Latin term. Her cult spread widely. Her figure has been found in England, France, and southern Germany. Some statuettes rest in temples, some in graves, and some were thrown as offerings into sacred springs.
objective: The nourishing goddess Dea Nutrix, her triple figure, and her wide cult across Roman Britain and the continent.
key_results: Dea Nutrix means "nourishing goddess" in Latin.
